prompt: You SSH into a server you have never touched before and a nightly job is failing. Name the first three places you look on the filesystem and say what each one tells you.
criteria: Names /var/log or a service log path as one of the three
Says what /etc holds and why config is checked before code
Gives a reason for each location rather than listing paths alone
Mentions checking free space or a full filesystem as a cause

prompt: A colleague's loader opens `config/settings.yml` and has never failed when they run it by hand from their project folder. Scheduled in cron, it dies on the first night. What breaks first, and why did the manual run hide it?
criteria: States that the path is resolved against the working directory
Says cron starts the job somewhere else, often the home directory
Names an absolute path or an explicit cd as the fix
Explains that the manual run happened to start in the right place

prompt: A script runs `cd /srv/reports`, then `cd ../etl`, then `pwd`. What does `pwd` print?
Match each directory on an unfamiliar Linux box to what you would expect to find there.
right: The record of what a job did the last time it ran
Scratch space that may be wiped on reboot
Executables placed there by the package manager
One person's own files and dotfiles

prompt: A deploy script ends with the line `chmod -R 777 /srv/app/uploads`, under a comment reading "fixes permission errors". Critique that line.
criteria: States that 777 makes the tree writable by every local account
Says the real question is which user the service runs as
Names chown plus a narrower mode such as 750 as the fix
Points out that -R also marks every file below as executable

prompt: A contractor messages you: "I keep getting Permission denied writing to the shared export folder — just put me in sudo and I'll stop bothering you." Write your reply.
criteria: Names group membership or directory ownership as the smaller fix
States that sudo grants the whole machine, not one folder
Asks for the exact path and the error text before changing anything
Offers a concrete next step instead of a flat no

prompt: A file listed as `-rw-r-----` is owned by user `alice` and group `analysts`. A member of `analysts` who is not alice may ____ the file but may not ____ it.
This provisioning snippet sets up a service account and its credentials. Exactly one line is a real security bug — which one?
why: The directory holding the database credentials is left writable by every account on the box. The 600 mode on the last line protects the contents of db.conf, but a world-writable parent directory lets any local user delete that entry and drop in their own file, which the service will then read. This directory wants chmod 700.

prompt: A client's office manager emails: "Please send over your SSH key so IT can set up your access." Write the reply you would actually send.
criteria: Sends the public key and names the .pub file explicitly
States that the private half never leaves your machine
Explains the reason in one line without a lecture on cryptography
Ends with a concrete next step or a question about where to send it

prompt: A team keeps one private key file in the shared password manager, and every new hire downloads that file to get onto the servers. Critique the arrangement.
criteria: States that a shared private key destroys per-person attribution
Says revoking one leaver's access means rotating it for everyone
Names one key pair per person as the alternative
Notes that the key now exists on every machine anyone copied it to

prompt: True or false: an attacker who obtains a copy of the `authorized_keys` file from a server can use it to log in as that user. Justify the verdict.
criteria: States that authorized_keys contains public keys only
Says login requires the matching private key, which the file lacks
Describes the client signing a challenge to prove possession
Notes that write access to that file would be the real danger

prompt: Which of these statements about an SSH key pair hold up?
options: The public half is what gets copied onto each server you want to reach
If you lose the private half you can regenerate it from the public half
A passphrase on the private key limits the damage if the laptop is stolen
During the handshake the server proves it holds your private key
One key pair can authorise you on any number of unrelated servers

prompt: You read a model's walkthrough of a tricky query plan, follow every step, and close the tab satisfied. The next day you cannot reconstruct the argument. Explain what actually happened.
criteria: Names recognition and production as two separate abilities
States that following an argument leans on the text as a crutch
Says retrieval from a blank page is the step that was skipped
Gives a way to test the difference before closing the tab

prompt: A teammate says deliberate practice on fundamentals is a waste of time now, because anything can be looked up in seconds. Give them your honest counter.
criteria: Concedes that lookup is fine for facts you can look up
Names a moment where lookup is unavailable, such as a live conversation
States that fluency comes from retrieval, not from access
Stops short of claiming memorisation beats understanding

prompt: You have two free hours the day before a technical conversation about a topic you half know. Which use of them leaves you most able to talk about it?
options: Re-reading your notes twice with a highlighter
Watching a recorded talk on the topic
Writing an explanation from memory, then checking it and closing the gaps
Skimming the documentation index until the terms feel familiar

prompt: Put these steps in the order that turns a page you have read into something you can say out loud.
items: Compare your version against the source and mark what you missed
Read the explanation once, then close it
Come back later and drill only the parts you missed
Write the explanation from a blank page without looking

prompt: Two copies of the same worker get started on one box — one from a systemd unit, one from a tmux session someone left running — and both are configured to listen on port 9000. What breaks first, and what does the copy that survives see?
criteria: States that only one process can hold the listening socket
Says the second start fails with address already in use
Notes that the first listener keeps serving traffic untouched
Points out the surviving process shows no sign of the conflict

prompt: Binding a service to 0.0.0.0 is the default in most tutorials. Name the cases where it is the wrong choice, and say what you would bind to instead.
criteria: States that 0.0.0.0 accepts connections on every interface
Names a database, admin panel or metrics port as a case to keep local
Gives 127.0.0.1 as the bind address for same-host callers
Mentions a proxy or an SSH tunnel as how remote callers still reach it

prompt: An app on a server is bound to `127.0.0.1:8080`. Logged into that server, `curl localhost:8080` returns a page, but a load balancer on another host times out. What is going on?
options: Another process has already taken port 8080
The listener accepts connections only over the loopback interface
The load balancer has to authenticate before it can connect
Port 8080 is reserved and cannot be reached from off the host

prompt: A service refuses to start with "address already in use" on a box several teams share. Order the steps for tracking it down.
items: Restart the service and confirm it is listening where you expect
Read the error to get the exact address and port it wanted
Decide whether the process holding the port should be running at all
Run `ss -ltnp` to find which process currently holds it
Stop that process or move the new service to a different port

prompt: Leadership asks how long it would take to have the warehouse serving queries again if the primary cluster vanished this morning. Give your estimate and show how you got there.
criteria: Gives a range rather than a single confident number
Splits the number into provision, restore, replay and verify
Names what the estimate hangs on, such as data volume or archive location
States that the figure is a guess until a drill measures it

prompt: Your manager points out that the nightly snapshot job has exited green for 400 days straight, so spending a sprint day on a restore rehearsal is hard to justify. Respond.
criteria: Separates the job exiting zero from the archive being usable
Names one failure a green job would never catch
Proposes a time-boxed drill rather than an open-ended project
Asks what recovery time the business is actually assuming

prompt: This cron script has been reporting success every night for a year. Exactly one line is why the backups may be worthless — which one?
why: A shell pipeline reports the exit status of its last command, so `set -e` sees gzip succeed even when pg_dump dies partway. The script writes a perfectly valid gzip file containing a truncated dump, exits zero, and the next line then deletes the older archives that were still restorable. Add `set -o pipefail`, or dump to a file and check the status before compressing.

prompt: True or false: a backup job that has reported success every night for a year is evidence that you can restore from it. Justify the verdict.
criteria: Distinguishes the job finishing from the data coming back
Names something a green job misses, such as a truncated or unreadable archive
States that only a performed restore counts as evidence
Says the drill has to produce a measured elapsed time
